Create a directory `efs` that you will use as the file system mount point using the following command:\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mkdir efs\\\\n ```\\\\n3. Run one of the following commands to mount your file system.\\\\n\\\\n **Note:**\\\\n\\\\n If the EC2 instance and the file system you are mounting are located in different\\\\n AWS Regions, see Mounting EFS file systems from a different AWS Region to edit the `region` property in\\\\n the `efs-utils.conf` file.\\\\n\\\\n * To mount using the file system id:\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs file-system-id efs-mount-point/\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n Use the ID of the file system you are mounting in place `file-system-id` and `efs` in place of `efs-mount-point`.\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs fs-abcd123456789ef0 efs/\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n Alternatively, if you want to use encryption of data in transit, you can mount your\\\\n file system with the following command.\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/\\\\n ```\\\\n * To mount using the file system DNS name:\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls file-system-dns-name efs-mount-point/\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0.efs.us-east-2.amazonaws.com efs/\\\\n ```\\\\n * To mount using the mount target IP address:\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n sudo mount -t efs -o tls,mounttargetip=mount-target-ip file-system-id efs-mount-point/\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/mounting-fs-mount-helper-ec2-linux.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Tutorial: Create an EFS file system and mount it on an EC2 instance using the AWS CLI\",\"context\":\"### Step 3.3: Mount the file system on your EC2 instance and test\\\\n\\\\nNow you mount the file system on your EC2 instance.\\\\n\\\\n1. You can\\\\n optionally specify the IP address of the mount target directly.\\\\n\\\\n ```\\\\n $ sudo mount -t nfs -o nfsvers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2,noresvport mount-target-ip:/ ~/efs-mount-point\\\\n ```\\\\n3. {"id": "31d2a837-f12d-4bfd-b972-6f7f0e650be2", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the standard way to mount an EFS file system on an EC2 Linux instance, using the recommended **EFS mount helper** (preferred over plain NFS since it handles TLS and retries for you):

**1. Install the EFS mount helper** (if not already present)
```
sudo yum -y install amazon-efs-utils      # Amazon Linux / RHEL
# or
sudo apt-get -y install amazon-efs-utils  # Ubuntu/Debian
```

**2. Create a mount point directory**
```
sudo mkdir efs
```

**3. Mount the file system**

- By file system ID (simplest):
  ```
  sudo mount -t efs fs-abcd123456789ef0 efs/
  ```
- With encryption in transit (recommended):
  ```
  sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/
  ```
- Using an access point:
  ```
  sudo mount -t efs -o tls,accesspoint=fsap-0123456789abcdef0 fs-abcd123456789ef0:/ efs/
  ```

**Prerequisites before mounting:**
- A mount target must exist for the file system in the EC2 instance's AZ/VPC.
- The mount target's security group must allow inbound NFS (port 2049) from the instance's security group.
- The instance needs network reachability to the mount target (same VPC, or peered/connected).

If you want it to persist across reboots, add an entry to `/etc/fstab`, e.g.:
```
fs-abcd123456789ef0 efs _efs _netdev,tls 0 0
```

Let me know the file system ID or instance you're working with if you'd like me to check mount targets, security group rules, or connectivity for your setup.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
